# Runbook

How to build this from nothing, what every target is for, and what to do when it
breaks. Measured figures are placeholders rendered from
`web/public/data/manifest.json`; commands and paths are literal.

The build in this repository right now used the `{{ raw:backend }}` backend,
over the window {{ month:window.start }} to {{ month:window.end }}, with
{{ month:window.detail_month }} published at trip grain: {{ n:source_files }}
source files, {{ n:months }} months, {{ n:services }} services.

## Before anything

```
uv sync --all-extras
cd web && npm ci && cd ..
uv run cityflow doctor
```

`make install` does the first two. `doctor` is the third because it reports what
this machine can and cannot do **before** a build fails halfway through: the
repository root it resolved, whether the zone reference and the zone shapefile
are present, whether `curl`, `dbt` and `node` are on the PATH, and whether a
warehouse already exists. It exits non zero if anything is missing, and each row
carries the command that fixes it.

`dbt` is a workspace dependency, so it arrives with `uv sync` and every
invocation goes through `uv run`. There is no separate dbt install.

## The zone shapefile

Everything geographic starts here, and it is the one input that is not
reproducible from code.

The official TLC taxi zone shapefile is published as `taxi_zones.zip` from the
NYC TLC trip record data page, `https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/about/tlc-trip-record-data.page`,
on the same CloudFront distribution that serves the trip parquet
(`https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/misc/taxi_zones.zip`). Take the link
from the page rather than hardcoding the path: the direct path has moved before
and the page is the authoritative pointer.

Unpack it so that the shapefile and its siblings sit at:

```
raw/zones/taxi_zones.shp
raw/zones/taxi_zones.dbf
raw/zones/taxi_zones.shx
raw/zones/taxi_zones.prj
```

`cityflow zones` looks for the stem `raw/zones/taxi_zones` and exits with code
two and a pointer to this document if it is not there.

**It is not committed, and `raw/` is in `.gitignore`.** It is a third party
artifact with its own terms, it is fetched from one URL, and a binary blob in
version control that nobody diffs is a binary blob that nobody notices going
stale. What **is** committed is everything derived from it:
`data/reference/dim_zone.csv`, which is the zone dimension the warehouse seeds
from and which the generator draws its zone list from, and
`web/public/data/zones.geojson`, which the map reads. Both are regenerated by
`cityflow zones` and both should be reviewed in the diff when they change, which
is what `assert_dim_zone_counts` is there to force.

### The stand in, and why there is one

Because the real file cannot be committed, every test that touched the geometry
module was guarded by a skip, and a skip reports green. On a runner all of them
skipped at once and the module ran at 41 percent coverage: the lowest figure in
the repository, in the one module where a silent fan out had already shipped.

`scripts/build_zone_fixture.py` writes a shapefile with the same structure and
the same defects, built from the committed zone reference so the two cannot
drift: the same {{ n:shapefile_polygon_records }} polygon records over the same
{{ n:shapefile_zone_ids }} zone ids, the same {{ n:shapefile_multi_part_zones }}
zones split across several records, and the same ids with no polygon at all. It
is the same tactic as the trip generator, applied to geometry.

```
uv run python scripts/build_zone_fixture.py raw/zones/taxi_zones
```

It is not a map. Every polygon in it is a circle, positioned on the real
centroid and sized to the real area, and nothing derived from it says anything
about New York. It exists so that the dissolve, the geometryless ids, the
unknown codes and the simplification tolerance are all exercised on a machine
that does not have the real file, which is every machine in continuous
integration. The geometry tests run against it always and against the real file
additionally, whenever the real file is present.

## A clean build against the real TLC data

```
git clone <repo> && cd cityflow
make install
# unpack taxi_zones.zip into raw/zones/ as above
uv run cityflow doctor

make zones
CITYFLOW_BACKEND=tlc uv run cityflow ingest      # or: make ingest-tlc
make transform
make publish
make reconcile
make docs
make gates
make web
```

Notes on that sequence.

`CITYFLOW_BACKEND` is the only configuration value with an environment
override, so the same committed `config/cityflow.yml` builds either warehouse
without an edit. Everything else is a property of the build and belongs in
version control where a reviewer can see it. To change it permanently, edit
`backend:` in the config.

The window comes from `config/cityflow.yml`. The committed window starts before
the airport fee appears on purpose, so that a real schema change sits inside the
build and `assert_surcharge_null_before_introduction` is not passing vacuously.
A window entirely inside one vintage proves nothing about the vintage mapping.

`cityflow ingest` fetches each month with `curl`, lands it, and deletes the
source file. Pass `--keep-source` when you are iterating on the normalizer and
re-resolving every month is the slow part. Expect this to take hours and tens of
gigabytes of transfer for a multi year window across three services; the
high volume for hire files dominate both.

`make transform` runs `dbt seed` then `dbt build`, which builds the models and
runs every test, including the nine singular assertions in `transform/tests`.

`make publish` builds the shipped aggregates, runs the analysis step (STL, PELT,
the Wilson intervals and the corrected zone comparisons), writes the metric
catalog and the lineage, and then writes the manifest. The size budget is
checked inside it, before it returns.

`make docs` re-renders every document from the manifest. `make gates` then
checks them, along with everything else.

## A clean build against the generator

```
make install
# raw/zones/taxi_zones.shp is still required: the generator draws from the real zone list
make zones
make ingest-synthetic            # or: make ingest SCALE=0.01 for a small one
make transform publish reconcile docs
```

No network is needed past `uv sync` and `npm ci`. `SCALE` is a fraction of full
volume and is honoured by the synthetic backend only; CI uses `--scale 0.002`,
which puts the whole pipeline inside a CI minute while still exercising every
vintage, every quarantine rule and every aggregate.

The generator still needs `data/reference/dim_zone.csv`, so `make zones` and
therefore the shapefile is a prerequisite either way. It draws from the real
zone list because a synthetic geography would not exercise the real join, which
is the thing that has broken before.

Everything the generator does and does not reproduce is in
[data.md](data.md), under Provenance. Read it before quoting any figure this
path produces.

## Every target

| target | what it does | when you want it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `install` | `uv sync --all-extras` and `npm ci` | once per checkout, and after a dependency change |
| `doctor` | reports what this machine can do | before a long build, and first when something fails oddly |
| `zones` | shapefile to `dim_zone.csv` and `zones.geojson` | after unpacking the shapefile, or after changing the simplification tolerance |
| `ingest` | resolves, normalizes, quarantines and lands every month for the configured backend | the first stage of any build |
| `ingest-tlc` | the same, forcing the real files | when the config default is `synthetic` and you want the real warehouse |
| `ingest-synthetic` | the same, forcing the generator | on a machine with no egress, in CI, and for any test of the rules themselves |
| `transform` | `dbt seed` then `dbt build` | after ingest, and after any model change |
| `publish` | shipped aggregates, analysis, catalog, lineage, manifest | after transform, and after any metric or aggregate change |
| `pipeline` | `zones ingest transform publish reconcile docs` | a full rebuild in one command |
| `lint` | ruff, ruff format, `mypy --strict`, sqlfluff, the dash gate | before every commit |
| `test` | pytest with an eighty percent coverage floor | before every commit |
| `reconcile` | every metric from the warehouse and from the shipped layer | after publish, always |
| `claims` | re-derives every published figure and diffs the documents | after publish, and in CI |
| `docs` | renders the documents from the manifest | when `claims` fails for a reason you have read and accepted |
| `size` | per file and total budget over the shipped directory | after publish, and in CI |
| `metric-gate` | scans the page for a metric computed outside the layer | after touching anything in `web/src` |
| `palette` | eight scale runs, both modes | after touching a colour |
| `gates` | all of the above gates in order | before opening a pull request |
| `web` | `npm run lint`, `typecheck` and `build` | after any dashboard change |
| `web-dev` | the dashboard on a local dev server | while working on a panel |
| `web-test` | the Playwright smoke test against the built export | after `web`; it also writes the query log the bench script folds in |
| `bench` | latency, bytes pulled and row groups skipped across {{ n:bench_queries }} panel queries | after changing an aggregate's grain, sort key or row group size |
| `clean` | removes the warehouse and build output, keeps the shipped layer | when you want to rebuild from source without re-downloading the shipped layer |
| `all` | `pipeline gates web web-test` | the whole thing, in order |

`make help` prints the same list from the Makefile itself.

## Failure modes that actually happen

### The egress policy denies the TLC host

**Symptom.** `SourceUnavailableError` out of `SourceRegistry._download`, carrying
the URL, the curl exit code and curl's stderr.

**Tell it apart from a flaky network.** `curl` is invoked with three retries and
a delay. A transient failure usually succeeds on a retry or fails differently
each time. A policy denial fails immediately, identically, on every attempt, and
typically as an HTTP 403 or a DNS failure rather than a timeout. Check it
directly:

```
curl -I https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/trip-data/yellow_tripdata_2024-06.parquet
```

**What to do.** Either add the host to the allowlist, or run with
`CITYFLOW_BACKEND=synthetic`, which needs no network at all. The error message
says this. It is the reason the committed default is the generator: a default
that cannot run on the machine the repository was written on is not a default.

**A different failure with a similar look.** If `curl` is not on the PATH at all,
the registry says so by name before attempting anything, because the `tlc`
backend depends on it for resume and atomic rename. `cityflow doctor` reports it
as its own row.

### The DuckDB memory limit is set above physical memory

**Symptom.** The process disappears partway through a fact table build. No Python
traceback, no DuckDB error, exit status 137. `dmesg` shows the kernel OOM killer.
The build often gets further on a second attempt, which makes it look flaky.

**Why.** DuckDB spills to `temp_directory` when it reaches the limit **you**
configured. It is killed by the kernel when it reaches the limit the **machine**
has. So a limit at or above physical memory is not a larger budget. It removes
the only mechanism that would have saved the build, and converts a slow query
into a crash.

**What to do.** Set `duckdb_memory_limit` in `config/cityflow.yml` below
physical memory, leaving room for the rest of the machine. This build ran at
`{{ raw:memory_limit }}`. Then set the same value in `transform/profiles.yml`,
because the Python side and dbt each open their own connection and there are
genuinely two places. Check that
`warehouse/tmp` is on a filesystem with room to spill into; that path is set in
both files too, and a spill directory that fills up produces a different and
clearer error. `preserve_insertion_order: false` is set in both for the same
reason: preserving it costs memory that buys nothing here.

Raise the limit only on a machine with more memory, and raise both copies.

### A shipped file is over budget

**Symptom, during publish.** `build_all` raises with the file name and its size
against the {{ f0:file_budget_mb }} MB per file budget, before it returns and
before anything is committed.

**Symptom, in CI.** `make size` fails against the committed directory and prints
every file with its size, the per file budget and the total.

**Why the budget exists.** GitHub refuses a file over a hundred megabytes and
warns past fifty. A repository that serves its own demo from Pages has a hard
per file ceiling, and finding it at push time after a full rebuild is the
expensive way.

**What to do.** Coarsen the aggregate's grain, or narrow the window in
`config/cityflow.yml`, and rebuild. **Do not split the file.** Splitting a file
to get under a per file limit is dodging the budget rather than meeting it, and
the check says so in its own failure message. If it is the total budget that
failed rather than a single file, treat it as the signal it is: a shipped layer
that keeps growing means the aggregate grain has drifted towards the fact table,
and the fix is upstream of the file.

This build ships {{ f2:shipped_mb }} MB across {{ n:shipped_files }} files
against a {{ f0:total_budget_mb }} MB total budget, largest file
{{ f2:largest_shipped_mb }} MB against a {{ f0:file_budget_mb }} MB per file
budget. The file to watch as the window grows is `agg_od_flow.parquet`, now
{{ f2:mb.agg_od_flow_parquet }} MB, because an origin to destination matrix is
quadratic in zones.

### The claim gate disagrees

**Symptom.** `make claims` prints, per document, a unified diff between the
committed file and the re-derived one.

**Read the diff first.** That is the entire point of the gate. A number that
moved is either a number you expected to move, because you widened the window,
switched backend, or changed a definition, or it is a number that moved for a
reason you do not yet know. Those two cases look identical until you read them,
and only one of them should be committed.

**If the move is expected:** `make docs` re-renders, and the manifest and the
documents go into the same commit. They are a pair. Committing a re-rendered
document without the manifest that produced it makes the next run of the gate
fail for a reason that has nothing to do with the change.

**Other failures from the same gate.** `<file> has not been rendered` means a
template exists with no output; run `make docs`. A `ClaimError` means one of
three things, and the message says which: the template names a claim id that
does not exist (it lists the ones that do); the template uses a format that does
not exist (it lists those too); or the claim is null in the manifest, which
means the query behind it returned nothing and the document therefore cannot
state it. Do not work around the last one by typing the number. Fix the query or
remove the sentence.

**Never hand edit a rendered document.** `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/data.md`,
`docs/metrics.md`, `docs/statistics.md` and `docs/runbook.md` are outputs. The
sources are in `docs/templates/`, mirroring the same paths. An edit to an output
is reverted by the next `make docs` and fails the gate in between.

### Reconcile disagrees

**Symptom.** `cityflow reconcile` exits non zero and prints a table of metric,
grain, key, warehouse value and browser value.

**Read the grain column first.** It localises the bug faster than anything else.

- Disagreement at `by service and month` but not at `overall`: a grain bug. A
  filter dropped from an aggregate, or a join that fans out for one service,
  cancels in the sum and does not cancel in the parts. This is the case the four
  grain check exists for and the reason it is not one check.
- Disagreement at every grain including `overall`: the two expressions are
  computed over different populations. Compare the `warehouse` and `browser`
  expressions in `metrics/metrics.yml` side by side; one of them has forgotten
  its own filter. Remember that `filters` is a comment and is never applied, so
  the population must be inside each expression.
- A value on one side and `None` on the other: a key exists in one source and
  not the other. Usually the aggregate was built from an older warehouse.

**The most common false alarm** is a stale shipped layer. The rebuild order is
`make transform`, then `make publish`, then `make reconcile`, and reconciling
against aggregates built before the last dbt run will disagree for a reason that
is not a bug. If you are unsure, republish and re-run before investigating.

If `zone_comparisons.parquet` or `agg_zone_hour.parquet` is missing entirely,
reconcile raises a `FileNotFoundError` naming the file and telling you to
publish first, rather than reporting a pass over nothing.

### A dbt incremental that only works on full refresh

**Symptom.** `dbt build` passes after `--full-refresh` and
`assert_fct_trip_row_count_matches_staging` fails on a plain incremental run.
That test prints the staged count and the fact count, and the difference between
them is the shape of the problem.

**The predicate, and why it is what it is.** `fct_trip` is incremental with no
`unique_key`, because the ingest assigns `trip_id` and never reissues one, so
there is nothing to merge on. Its predicate is an anti join on `source_period`:
the model takes every source period the target does not already hold. It is
deliberately not "greater than the newest loaded month", because a month arrives
whole, from one published file, and comparing against the maximum would silently
refuse a backfill of an older month. That is exactly the case where an
incremental model loses data without erroring.

**The failure this predicate actually produces.** `cityflow ingest` appends. It
does not consult `source_audit` before landing a month, so running it a second
time over a window that is already loaded lands those months into `stg_trip`
twice. Staging then doubles for those periods, `fct_trip` refuses the rows
because it already holds those source periods, and
`assert_fct_trip_row_count_matches_staging` fails with a fact count short of
staging by exactly the duplicated months. The test failure is the symptom. The
cause is one stage upstream, and `mart_source_freshness` will show two audit
rows for the same service and period, which is the confirmation.

**What to do.**

1. Do not reach for `--full-refresh` as the fix. It makes the failure disappear
   and leaves a model that is incremental in name and full rebuild in practice,
   which is a much more expensive problem discovered much later.
2. Check `mart_source_freshness` for duplicate audit rows.
3. If the ingest ran twice, rebuild the warehouse: `uv run cityflow ingest
   --fresh` drops it and starts over. That is the supported way to re-run a
   window.
4. If the counts are clean and the test still fails, look at
   `assert_fct_trip_zone_join_does_not_fan` in the same run. It prints three
   counts: staged, rejoined and fact. If staged and rejoined differ, the zone
   dimension has gained a duplicate key and the problem is in `cityflow zones`,
   not in the incremental at all.

Use `--full-refresh` deliberately, when a model's SQL has changed in a way that
alters already loaded rows. Never as a way past a failing test.

## The monthly refresh

`.github/workflows/refresh.yml` runs on a schedule around the middle of the
month, after the TLC has published the previous month, and on manual dispatch
with a backend input.

What it does, in order:

1. Copies the current `manifest.json` aside, so there is a before to diff
   against.
2. Rebuilds the whole warehouse from the real files:
   `zones`, `ingest`, `dbt seed`, `dbt build`, `publish`, `manifest`,
   `reconcile`. If reconcile fails, the job fails and no pull request is opened,
   which is the correct behaviour: a refresh that cannot prove the shipped layer
   agrees with the warehouse has nothing to offer.
3. Re-renders every document from the new manifest.
4. Diffs the two manifests claim by claim and writes a Markdown table.
5. Opens a pull request on the branch `refresh/monthly`.

**What the pull request contains.** The changed files under
`web/public/data/**`, plus `README.md`, `RESULTS.md` and `docs/**`. The body is
the figure diff: one row per claim that moved, with the claim id, the value
before, the value after and the percentage change, or `No published figure
changed.` when nothing moved.

That body is the reason the workflow exists in this shape. A dashboard that
refreshes itself silently is a dashboard nobody audits. A pull request whose
description is a list of every published number that moved, and by how much, is
something a reviewer can actually approve or reject: a new month appearing is
expected, a tip rate moving by a tenth of a percent is expected, and a
quarantine share doubling is a conversation that happens before the number goes
live rather than after somebody notices.

The workflow has a long timeout because a full rebuild against the real files is
measured in hours. It is scheduled rather than triggered on publication because
there is nothing to subscribe to.

## Deployment

`.github/workflows/pages.yml` builds the dashboard and deploys it to GitHub
Pages on a push to `main` that touches `web/**`.

It does not rebuild the warehouse. The shipped layer is committed, so the Pages
build serves exactly the data a reader of the repository sees, on a runner that
could not hold the warehouse anyway. That is also why the size budget is a gate
rather than a guideline.

### The host does not always serve the bytes it says it is serving

GitHub Pages gzip compresses parquet responses, and for some objects its edge
answers a byte range out of the compressed representation while labelling the
response with the uncompressed length. The first few kilobytes arrive as
zeroes, the tail arrives correct, and the reported total size is right, so
nothing upstream notices.

Measured on the deployed site, on two of the {{ n:shipped_files }} shipped
files at once: a whole file `GET` returned the correct bytes and the correct
SHA-256 while a `bytes=0-3` `GET` against the same URL in the same second
returned four zero bytes. A redeploy did not clear it. The copies in the
repository were intact throughout, and `make size` and `make claims` both
passed, because neither of them reads the deployed site.

What a reader saw was three tiles reading `no data`, two charts showing
`Invalid Error: TProtocolException: Invalid data`, and no indication of which
file or why. DuckDB reads the footer at the end of the file, which was correct,
then seeks to a column chunk near the start, which was zeroes, and fails inside
the Thrift parser that is trying to parse a page header out of them.

`src/lib/duckdb-client.ts` now asks each file for its first four bytes before
registering it and checks them against the parquet magic. A file that answers
correctly is registered as a URL and read by range, which is the whole point of
the architecture and what the {{ f1:shipped_mb }} MB layer is designed around. A
file that does not is fetched whole, which this host does serve correctly, and
the fallback is reported on the data health panel rather than hidden, because
every other panel on that page tells the reader it reads by range and on a
broken host that would be false.

The cost of the check is four bytes per file, in parallel, at boot.

`web/tests/delivery.spec.ts` reproduces the fault rather than describing it: it
intercepts ranged reads of one file and returns zeroes of the right length with
the right headers, exactly as the host did, then asserts that the page falls
back for that file and only that file, that every tile still renders a number,
that no query fails, and that the page says so. Disabling the check makes it
fail, which was verified before it was committed.

If this starts happening to a file large enough that fetching it whole is not
acceptable, the answer is to move the shipped layer to a host that serves
ranges correctly, and to say on the README that the demo is no longer served
from the repository alone.

Two properties of the export are enforced in CI rather than assumed. The `web`
job greps the built output for any third party origin and fails if one appears:
the page must be self contained, both because this network cannot reach a CDN
and because a deployed public page should not depend on one. And `duckdb-wasm`
is pinned below the release in which the parquet reader became an extension
fetched at first use from an external host, which would be unreachable here and
an uncontrolled dependency everywhere else.
